objectives: Set up your computer so it is comfortable and easy to use.
Spot a scam or a fake identity and check it a safer way.
Protect your devices and files with updates, permissions, locking and passwords.
Show five skills from this course, then take the post-test.
outcomes: Comfort and access: at a lab workstation, each learner makes one comfort change (chair, screen distance, text size or Magnifier) and says what it made easier, then names two universal design features and who each one helps. The change is visible, and lab settings are restored afterwards.

Scams: given the fictional message on slide 8, each learner names two warning signs and an independent check that does not use the message’s link or number, says what to do after typing a password, and gives a safe next step for a catfishing request, fear of missing out and a hurtful post, with no more than one prompt.

Devices and files: using slide 9, Edge settings, Windows Update and Word’s Protect Document menu without changing anything, each learner chooses safe responses to an unknown USB drive and an unneeded camera request, says why updates matter, tells a password to open (encryption) apart from read-only, and says what device encryption protects and when to lock the screen. Both knowledge checks are answered correctly.

Skills challenge and post-test: working alone, each learner completes the five challenge rows (refined search, structured paragraph, formula total, undo recovery, useful feedback), each rated Independent, With prompt or Needs practice, then completes the 28-question post-test and records the score and one next practice task.
agenda: Warm-up and reconnect

Reconnect: two or three learners share last week’s home task. Recall from earlier weeks: what does two-step verification add to a password (week 4), and does read-only keep a file secret (week 2)? Pairs share slide 2: one habit that protects their work and one that makes the computer comfortable. Ask who has had an urgent text or email demanding action, without sharing private details.
Introduction: pause, inspect, verify

Read the four goals on slide 1 aloud and say how the day runs: safety habits first, then the skills challenge and the post-test. Play chapter 1: pause, inspect the evidence, verify independently. This routine is the Review question for every cycle.
Cycle A: comfort, access and attention

Tell: slides 3, 4 and 5 (screen about an arm’s length away with the top at or slightly below eye level; universal design; FOMO). Show: chapter 2, pausing at 1:23 so each learner picks one control; then on the projector, Magnifier (Windows logo key and +, close with Windows logo key and Esc) and the Notifications page in Settings. Do: worksheet tasks 1 and 2, every learner at their own seat. Review: a partner says what changed and why it helps; settings are put back.
Cycle B: scams and fake identities

Tell: slide 8 (phishing is a fake message pretending to be a trusted organization), then slides 6 and 7. Show: chapter 3, then chapter 4; pause at 2:43 and take a show of hands, reply or known route, before the answer plays. Play chapter 8. Live: point to a link on any webpage without clicking and read where it goes. Do: every learner inspects the subject, sender and link on slide 8, then writes worksheet tasks 3 and 4. Review: play chapter 9 and pause at 6:13; each learner tells a partner the evidence, what is unverified and the next step before the answer plays. Flip slide 9 card 3.
Cycle C: protect devices and files

Tell: slides 12 and 13, then slides 10 and 11 (a password to open encrypts a Word file; read-only only limits changes; Word cannot recover a lost password). Show: chapter 6, chapter 7 (pause at 4:55), then chapter 5 (pause at 3:36). Live: Edge Settings, search permissions, open Camera; then lock the screen with Windows logo key and L. Do: slide 9 cards 1, 2 and 4, then worksheet tasks 5 and 6, every learner, looking only. Review: the slide 16 and slide 17 knowledge checks; re-teach any choice that more than two learners miss.
Introduce the challenge
Play chapter 10, then show slide 15 and worksheet task 7. Say: five rows from weeks 2 to 4, done on your own; the quick card is allowed; a spoken prompt from anyone counts as With prompt.
Individual check: skills challenge

Every learner works the five rows of worksheet task 7 alone at their own seat; partners do not help. From minute 8, visit each learner once, about a minute each, and rate all five rows on the paper roster; come back once to anyone not finished. Check row 3 in the formula bar before the file is closed.
Break
Screen-free break. Finish any challenge ratings on the roster.
Post-test

Slide 18. Learners type their name first and work alone; read directions aloud without suggesting answers. A learner may enter the week 1 score from your roster for a comparison. Record each score out of 28; print page 1 only if a paper copy is needed. Late finishers may run to minute 110.
Apply and close

Slide 19: each learner reads the domain scores, completes worksheet task 8 and chooses one practice task; discuss the two or three items the class missed most. Slide 20. Home task: at home, check for updates or turn on two-step verification for one account, and share it at the start of week 6. Restore lab settings, then select Start fresh on this computer.
lab: Adjust one thing at your station so you can read without leaning in: chair height, screen distance (about an arm’s length) or text size. Or try Magnifier: press Windows logo key and +, then Windows logo key and Esc to close it. Write what you changed and what got easier, then put it back.

Play the first 10 seconds of the slide 14 video with the sound muted and read the captions. Then press Tab a few times and watch the outline move from control to control. Name two design features that help more people, and who each one helps.

On slide 8, select the subject, the sender and the link to inspect each one. Write two warning signs, the independent check you would use instead (a real website or a number you already trust), and what you would do if you had already typed your password.

Name the risk and one safe next step for each: (a) a new online friend asks you to keep a money request secret; (b) you stay up late scrolling because you do not want to miss anything; (c) someone posts something hurtful about you in a public group.

Say your choice for each card on slide 9 before you flip it. Then look without changing anything: in Edge, open Settings from the ··· menu, search permissions and open Camera; in Windows 10, open Start › Settings › Update & Security › Windows Update (Windows 11: Start › Settings › Windows Update). Write one thing each page shows.

In Word, open a blank document and select File › Info › Protect Document. Write which option asks for a password to open and encrypts the file, and which only limits changes. Do not set a password. Then write what device encryption protects and what you do before you step away from a signed-in computer.

Skills challenge, on your own: refine a search, build a structured paragraph, total four costs with a formula, bring back deleted text and write useful feedback. Leave your work on screen for your instructor.
Take the post-test on your own. Print page 1 of your results or save it as a PDF, and write your score out of 28. Name one strength and one skill to practice next.
answers: A specific change (chair, screen about an arm’s length away with the top at or slightly below eye level, text size or Magnifier) and a benefit the learner can see; no medical claims. Settings restored.

Universal design makes tools usable by more people without special changes. Examples: captions (noisy room, hearing loss), keyboard access (cannot use a mouse), clear text labels that do not rely on color.

Signs: pressure to act now, a sender or link that does not match the organization (account-check.example), a request for a password. Check: the real website from a bookmark or typed address, or a number from a card or letter, never the message’s link or number. If a password was typed: change it on the real site, turn on two-step verification and tell the instructor.

(a) Possible catfishing: send no money and keep no secrets; verify another way. (b) Fear of missing out: set a stopping point or quiet alerts with Do not disturb. (c) Do not reply in anger; keep screenshots if safe; report or block; talk to someone you trust.

USB: do not connect; give it to staff. Camera: deny when the task does not need it. Benefits fee: do not pay or use the link; VA never charges a fee to apply; call a number from VA.gov. Windows 10: free security updates ended October 2025; use Extended Security Updates or a supported device. One real detail from each page; nothing changed or installed.

Encrypt with Password sets a password to open and encrypts the file; Word cannot recover a lost password. Always Open Read-Only and Restrict Editing only limit changes; the text is still readable. Device encryption protects a lost or stolen computer that is turned off; lock the screen with Windows logo key and L before stepping away.

Rate each row Independent, With prompt or Needs practice on the paper roster, using the evidence list below. The quick card counts as Independent; any spoken prompt is With prompt. Keep this separate from the post-test score.
Page 1 printed or saved; score out of 28 on the roster; a named strength and a specific next task tied to a results domain.

slide_changes.title: A comfortable workstation
slide_changes.body: Set the screen about an arm’s length away, with the top at or slightly below eye level. Keep the keyboard and mouse close. Change position and take short breaks, and ask for help with discomfort that does not go away.

slide_changes.title: Universal design helps more people
slide_changes.body: Universal design means building tools that more people can use without special changes. Captions help in a noisy room or with hearing loss. Keyboard access helps people who cannot use a mouse, and clear text labels help people who cannot tell some colors apart.

slide_changes.title: Protect attention and wellbeing
slide_changes.body: FOMO means fear of missing out: the pull to keep checking so you do not miss anything. Choose which alerts you really need. Do not disturb can quiet the rest while you finish a task.

slide_changes.title: An online identity can be invented
slide_changes.body: Catfishing is using a fake identity to build trust, sometimes with stolen photos of real service members. Pressure for money, secrecy or personal information is a reason to pause and verify another way. Never send money or gift cards to someone you have not met in person.

slide_changes.title: An urgent message is not proof
slide_changes.body: Phishing is a fake message posing as a trusted organization. Warning signs: pressure to act now, a mismatched sender or link, a request for a password or money. Check through the real website or a number you trust. Typed a password already? Change it and turn on two-step verification.

slide_changes.title: Choose a safer next step
cards: An unknown USB drive is on the desk
Do not connect it, even to find the owner. Give it to the instructor or lab staff.
A calculator site asks for camera access
Deny it unless the task has a clear, trusted need.
A message says you must pay a fee to keep your VA benefits
Do not pay or use its link. VA says it never charges fees to apply for benefits and never threatens you by email. Call a number from VA.gov or your benefit letter.
Your home computer still runs Windows 10
Free security updates ended October 2025. Enroll in Extended Security Updates (until October 2027) or move to a supported device, then check Windows Update.

slide_changes.title: Encryption protects readable data
slide_changes.body: Encryption scrambles data so only someone with the key can read it. Device encryption (BitLocker in Windows, FileVault on a Mac) protects a lost computer that is turned off. A signed-in computer is open to anyone at the keyboard, so press Windows logo key and L when you step away.

slide_changes.title: Passwords protect different actions
slide_changes.body: In Word, Encrypt with Password sets a password to open and encrypts the file. Always Open Read-Only and Restrict Editing only limit changes; anyone can still read the text. Word cannot recover a lost password, so keep it somewhere safe, away from the file.

slide_changes.title: Unknown devices can carry risk
slide_changes.body: An unknown USB drive can carry malware: software made to harm a computer or steal information. Do not plug it in to find its owner; give it to lab staff. Keep Windows and your browser updated, because updates fix known security holes.

slide_changes.title: Control camera and microphone access
slide_changes.body: Allow the camera or microphone only when the task needs it and you trust the site. A permission can stay on after a call, so review it in your browser’s site permissions. Block requests unrelated to what you are doing.

slide_changes.title: Practice the whole routine
slide_changes.body: Skills challenge: on your own, show five skills from this course. Refine a search, build a structured paragraph, total four costs, bring back deleted text and write useful feedback. Leave your work on screen for your instructor.

slide_changes.title: Knowledge check: encryption
options: Shrink a file so it takes less space
Keep data unreadable without the key
Let people read a file but not change it
slide_changes.why: Encryption keeps data unreadable without the key. Shrinking a file is compression, and read-only only limits changes. Encryption also does not prove a sender or website is honest.

slide_changes.title: Knowledge check: camera access
slide_changes.body: After a video visit, your browser still lets the clinic’s website use your camera and microphone. What is a sensible next step?
options: Leave it; permissions end when the call ends
Review the permission and block it if not needed
Block the camera for every website on this computer
slide_changes.why: A site permission can stay on after the call. Review it in your browser’s site permissions and block it if you no longer need it. Blocking every site would also stop the video visits you need.

slide_changes.title: Take the post-test
slide_changes.body: Type your name first, then answer on your own. When you finish, print page 1 of your results or save it as a PDF, and give your score out of 28 to your instructor.

prep: Each station: Microsoft Edge, Word and Excel, and this lesson and worksheet; check that a downloaded .csv file opens in Excel. At the front: the projector with Edge, Word and Windows Settings, and a USB drive to hold up for slide 12 (never plug it in). Print a paper roster with each learner code, five challenge columns, the week 1 pre-test score and a post-test column, and bring the week 1 scores. The lab needs no accounts: the phishing message, camera prompt and file protections are course simulations or look-only steps, and two-step verification is a home task. Ask IT before class whether the lab’s Windows 10 computers get Extended Security Updates, because learners will ask. Check that Windows Update, Edge site permissions and Word’s Protect Document menu open under a learner login. Play chapters 4 and 7 with captions to check sound. After your own run-through, delete any help-desk.docx and supplies files you created and select Start fresh on this computer at each station. Keep 3–5 printed post-tests in case the network fails. No paid service, real purchase or new learner account is required.
lab_paths: Zoom in with Magnifier
Press Windows logo key and + to zoom in. Press Windows logo key and Esc to close Magnifier.
Quiet your notifications
Start › Settings › System › Notifications. Turn off apps you do not need. For a quiet hour, open the notification center and select the bell with zZ to turn on Do not disturb.
See where a link really goes
Point to the link without clicking and read the web address that appears. If it does not match the organization’s real website, do not open it.
Report a phishing email
Outlook.com: select the message, then Report › Report phishing. Gmail: open the message, select More (⋮) next to Reply, then Report phishing.
Turn on two-step verification (at home)
Microsoft account: go to account.microsoft.com/security, select Manage how I sign in, then under Additional security, Two-step verification, select Turn on.
Check for Windows updates
Start › Settings › Windows Update › Check for updates. If updates are listed, select Download & install. Windows 10: Start › Settings › Update & Security › Windows Update.
Review which websites can use your camera
In Edge, open Settings from the ··· menu and type permissions in the Search settings box. Open Camera to see which sites are allowed; select a site to change it to Block.
Lock the computer when you step away
Press Windows logo key and L. Sign in again when you come back.
Require a password to open a Word file
File › Info › Protect Document › Encrypt with Password. Type the password twice, then save. Word cannot recover a lost password.
Stop changes but not reading
File › Info › Protect Document › Always Open Read-Only, or Review › Restrict Editing. Anyone can still read and copy the text.
Check device encryption
Start › Settings › Privacy & security › Device encryption. If it is missing, the computer may not support it or you may be signed in as a standard user.
Bring back something you just deleted
Press Ctrl and Z right away. It works after you save, until you close the file. For a file saved in OneDrive, select the file name at the top, then Version history.
Total a column in Excel
Select the empty cell under the numbers, type =SUM(B2:B5) and press Enter. Select the cell again to see the formula in the formula bar.

Scams aimed at veterans are common. VA says it never charges a fee to apply for benefits and never pressures or threatens by email. Welcome stories, but stop anyone before they share real account details.

Many learners may still use Windows 10 at home. Free security updates ended October 2025; consumer Extended Security Updates run until October 2027, and Edge keeps updating on Windows 10 until at least October 2028. Know the lab's own status before class.
If you run long, move worksheet task 4 to home practice and show the Magnifier on the projector only; never shorten the challenge or the post-test.

challenge.intro: Work on your own at your computer. Do each row, write what you did, and leave your work on screen. Your instructor rates each row. The quick card counts as Independent; a spoken prompt from anyone counts as With prompt. This challenge is separate from the post-test score.
tasks: In Edge, search senior center hours. Change the search so it finds this year’s hours for the senior center in Beckley, West Virginia.
Adds a place (Beckley WV) and a time (the current year) to the search box, and says why the narrower search gives a more useful list.

In Word, explain how to reach the fictional Community library help desk: a title in the Heading 1 style, a numbered list of three steps and one warning line in bold. Save it in Documents as help-desk.docx.
The title uses Heading 1, the steps are a Word numbered list (select one number and all three highlight), and the warning line is bold.
Select Practice workbook data at the end of this worksheet to download a fresh supplies.csv and open it in Excel. Type Tape in A5 and 4 in B5. In B6, total all four costs with a formula.
B6 shows 29 and the formula bar shows =SUM(B2:B5) or =B2+B3+B4+B5, not a typed number. Check before the file is closed: a .csv file keeps the result, not the formula.
